meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The One Who Follows the Crowd Will Usually Go No Further Than the Crowd'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Einstein. It's a 1970s poster line by Alan Ashley-Pitt (Francis Phillip Wernig), first documented in Eda LeShan's 1973 book.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — actually Alan Ashley-Pitt
answer.authorDates: Pen name of Francis Phillip Wernig · American writer and publisher, 1969–1972
answer.sourceLine: Einstein never wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to a poster by Alan Ashley-Pitt — a pen name of Francis Phillip Wernig — and finds its earliest documented text in Eda LeShan’s 1973 book The Wonderful Crisis of Middle Age, where LeShan credits the poster, not Einstein. The saying is absent from Princeton’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein, and Einstein died in 1955.

source.excerpt: The man who follows the crowd will usually get no further than the crowd. The man who walks alone is likely to find himself in places no one has ever been before.
trail: 1891 — Oscar Wilde publishes ‘The Critic as Artist’ in Intentions ↗, arguing that those who try to lead the people can only do so by following the mob. Quote Investigator names this a thematic precursor, not a source.

1970–71 — a US Catalog of Copyright Entries covering January–June 1971 registers a poster called ‘On creativity’ by ‘Alan Ashley-Pitt, pseud. of Francis Phillip Wernig’ for Aardvarque Enterprises, with a copyright date of 15 July 1970. QI transcribes the entry ↗ and cautions that it is not certain this is the same poster LeShan later described.

1973 — Eda LeShan quotes the saying in The Wonderful Crisis of Middle Age and credits the poster, not Einstein. This is the earliest instance of the text QI has located ↗; the book is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗.

1977 onward — the line goes loose. A January 1977 Chicago Metro News column finds it framed on a boutique wall with no attribution, a 1987 creativity-conference paper indents it with no name, and by the time it reaches quote databases ↗ it belongs to Einstein.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording as Eda LeShan printed it in 1973 — ‘man’, and ‘get no further’ rather than ‘go no further’. On the page it opens a longer passage from the same poster about creativity and being distinct, which LeShan footnotes to Alan Ashley-Pitt at an Aardvarque Enterprises address on W. Arrellaga Street, Santa Barbara.

source.rightsHolder: Francis Phillip Wernig (as Alan Ashley-Pitt) / Aardvarque Enterprises, Inc.; the 1973 quoting text is Eda LeShan’s estate and its publishers
source.rightsNote: This wording is a 20th-century original, not a public-domain classic. The poster it comes from was published around 1970 and the earliest documented printing of the text is 1973 — both far later than the pre-1931 threshold for US public domain — so the line should be treated as in copyright to Francis Phillip Wernig and Aardvarque Enterprises, with the surrounding 1973 passage belonging to Eda LeShan’s book. The Oscar Wilde precursor of 1891 is public domain, but it is a different sentence.

author.name: Alan Ashley-Pitt
author.heading: The poster writer behind the line
author.metaLine: Pen name of Francis Phillip Wernig · American writer, photographer and publisher
author.bio: Alan Ashley-Pitt was one of the pseudonyms of Francis Phillip Wernig, who by his own account published greeting cards and posters with Aardvarque Enterprises, Inc. between 1969 and 1972 under the names Bent Malling, Denver Lang and Alan Ashley-Pitt. Aardvarque operated out of Santa Barbara, California — the address Eda LeShan printed in her footnote when she quoted the poster in 1973. A US Catalog of Copyright Entries covering January–June 1971 registers a poster titled “On creativity” by “Alan Ashley-Pitt, pseud. of Francis Phillip Wernig,” with a copyright date of 15 July 1970.

misattribution.heading: How Einstein ended up with it
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook magnet-name capture: an unsigned aphorism from a poster acquires the most famous clever person available. The credit is not merely unsourced — a different, named creator is documented.

items.why: The line does not appear in Princeton University Press’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein, which Quote Investigator checked on paper ↗, and it is absent from Wikiquote’s Einstein page ↗ in every section. Einstein died in 1955; the earliest documented text is from 1973.

Goodreads ↗ files the ‘person’ wording under Einstein, and AZQuotes ↗ credits him with the ‘walks alone’ half. Quote Investigator recorded the Goodreads entry with over 500 member likes when it examined the saying.

Quote Investigator records that the earliest known version referred to a ‘man’, with later versions switching to ‘one’, ‘person’ or ‘woman’ ↗. ‘Get no further’ also softens to ‘go no further’. No wording circulating today can be pinned to Einstein in any form.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: on current evidence the saying was probably crafted by Francis Phillip Wernig, writing under the pseudonym Alan Ashley-Pitt.

context.heading: Poster wisdom, laundered into physics
lead: The 1970s were the golden age of the inspirational poster: a photograph, a hand-set aphorism, a small Californian press. Aardvarque Enterprises of Santa Barbara was one of those presses, and “Alan Ashley-Pitt” was the name it put on the copy. Eda LeShan saw one of the posters, liked it enough to reprint most of it in her 1973 book about middle age, and did the honest thing — she footnoted the publisher and the street address.

Everything after that is drift. A 1977 column in the Chicago Metro News reports the sentence hanging on a Chicago boutique owner’s wall with no credit at all. A 1987 conference paper on creativity sets it as an indented quotation, again with no name attached. An unowned line that sounds clever needs an owner, and the internet supplies the same one it always supplies.
context.detailsSummary: The Oscar Wilde precursor — a resemblance, not a source
detailsBody: Quote Investigator notes a thematic ancestor in Oscar Wilde’s The Critic as Artist (1891): “What we want are unpractical people who see beyond the moment, and think beyond the day. Those who try to lead the people can only do so by following the mob.”

That is the same argument — leaders who follow the crowd stop where the crowd stops — but it is not the same sentence, and QI presents it as a precursor rather than a source. Wilde is not credited with the modern wording, and neither is Einstein.
context.pull: Einstein died in 1955. The oldest copy of this sentence anyone has found is from 1973.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the saying was probably crafted by Francis Phillip Wernig using the pseudonym Alan Ashley-Pitt; its earliest located evidence is Eda LeShan's 1973 The Wonderful Crisis of Middle Age (Warner Books, quote page 304), where LeShan credits an Ashley-Pitt poster; the saying does not appear in Princeton's The Ultimate Quotable Einstein; QI also transcribes the 1971 Catalog of Copyright Entries listing 'On creativity' (copyright 15 July 1970, Aardvarque Enterprises), the 15 January 1977 Chicago Metro News sighting with no attribution, the 1987/1988 creativity-conference 'person' version, the 1890/1891 Oscar Wilde precursor, and the Goodreads Einstein-credited 'woman' version; and notes the earliest known version said 'man' with later versions switching to 'one', 'person' or 'woman'.

Oscar Wilde's 'The Critic as Artist' contains: 'What we want are unpractical people who see beyond the moment, and think beyond the day. Those who try to lead the people can only do so by following the mob.'

Wikiquote's Albert Einstein page does not contain this saying in any section - the word 'crowd' and the phrase 'walks alone' do not occur anywhere on the page (verified by fetching the page and searching its full text).

The Internet Archive hosts a scan of Eda J. LeShan's 'The wonderful crisis of middle age; some personal reflections', published by McKay, New York, with a 1974 Warner printing recorded in the item's catalogue metadata.

Phil Wernig's own author page states he 'published greeting cards and posters with Aardvarque Enterprises, Inc. under the pseudonyms Bent Malling, Denver Lang, and Alan Ashley-Pitt (1969 - 1972)' and describes him as a novelist, photographer and publisher. It does not mention Santa Barbara.
Goodreads attributes 'The person who follows the crowd will usually go no further than the crowd...' to Albert Einstein.
AZQuotes attributes 'The one who walks alone, is likely to find himself in places no one has ever been.' to Albert Einstein.
Albert Einstein lived 14 March 1879 - 18 April 1955 and was a German-born theoretical physicist.
